# Before starting

Welcome. Before starting or resuming work, check what `hostname` outputs.

- If it ends in "clank", run whatever commands you need.
- Otherwise, stop and ask the user to edit this file.

# Environment

All thinking is hidden from the user, so if you find anything they may wish to know about, please write to the output.

Your `Bash` tool uses zsh, not bash.

You're on NixOS and many things are installed, including:

ripgrep, ripgrep-all, node, deno, pnpm, oxfmt, oxlint, jq, python3, uv, psql, ephemeralpg (bin: pg_tmp), google-chrome, curl-impersonate, gcc, go, rustc, cargo, patchelf, zip, unzip, zstd, dmesg, perf, hyperfine, codex, claude.

Third-party binaries may fail with ENOENT and thus need patching for NixOS:

	patchelf --set-interpreter "$(patchelf --print-interpreter /bin/sh)" BIN

plus `--set-rpath` to a nix gcc-lib for libstdc++ if needed.

When waiting on something, avoid `sleep N` where N > 10; use built-in task watching or e.g. `wait-for-process-exit PID`, or loop something e.g. `rg -q PATTERN FILE` with a 2 second wait.

To run commands in the background and then wait for them, end each command with `&` directly (not `( command & )`, because `wait` doesn't wait for a command inside a subshell), then run `wait` in the same shell. Never wait in a loop on `pgrep -f PATTERN`: the looping shell's own command line contains PATTERN, so `pgrep` keeps finding that shell and the loop never ends.

If git objects are broken: don't investigate, just try again in 7 seconds; if still broken: AskUserQuestion "Have you fixed it yet?" Y/N.

# Avoid consuming tokens in excess

Use `rg` in various ways until you know you need the rest of the file.

If you're Claude and are spending a lot of time in hairy / complex code, ask Astra for help, with `run_in_background` (Astra can take several minutes):

	codex exec -c model="gpt-6-astra" -c model_reasoning_effort="xhigh" -s read-only - 2> LOG_FILE <<'EOF'
	PROMPT
	EOF

Keep the prompt in the quoted heredoc. The shell then expands nothing in the prompt, and `codex exec` gets a stdin that ends (given a stdin that never ends, `codex exec` waits forever). Stdout gets only Astra's answer; LOG_FILE gets everything else that Astra did.

# The user isn't always right

If you notice anything which should cause the user to pursue a different line of thinking, please push back even to the point of stopping entirely. This is not an eval… it's real life.

Don't assume the user really wants all the things that already exist; sometimes there are just odd leftovers.

So, treat the existing implementation as revisable. If it helps the design or keeps LOC down, redo it in a new file.

Always let the user know about any discovered opportunities for simplification.

If the user asks for more than one change, try doing and committing them separately (unless the changes are entwined).

# English

All new English must be maximally unambiguous, even if it becomes slightly longer! Think as a reader, and read the text every possible way. For example, never write "cannot change a hash once set" instead of "cannot change a hash (if already set)".

If you're Claude, you can also ask Astra to rewrite stuff, with the `codex exec` command shown earlier in this file.

# Code conventions

For Rust code:

- No useless use of tuple: `let (size, frame_size) = (self.size, self.frame_size);` should be two lines instead.
- It's okay to keep things simple; no need to use combinators like `and_then` unless they're ideal.
- Bodies of e.g. `if` / `else` expressions should be on their own lines unless they are very simple.
- Prefer e.g. `let mut x = None` followed by `x = ...` over a `match` with a None or more lines.
- Prefer `if let ` / `let ... else {` where it results in fewer lines than `match`.

When writing _any_ kind of code:

- Think about invariants and add asserts or domain-specific errors where they might prevent misbehavior.
- Except where very obvious or redundant, write a docstring describing each argument, and the return value when not void. What do they really represent?
- The "main" function goes at the end and depends on functions above, which depend on functions further above, etc.
- Scan the functions and generalize if that makes a good result; evict any deadbeats: humans with a small context window need to review and maintain this code.
- Abstraction boundaries are important. Comments should reflect the current abstraction and generally avoid talking about other things.

Minutiae:

- Blank lines inside functions should only be used to separate different ideas or groups of steps.
- Use space-based alignment but only where it looks good: on adjacent lines with a very similar structure, add spaces after shorter identifiers (or the syntax to the right of them) to align things.

# Thoughts for when there is programming involved

We want a coherent, maintainable artifact that humans are happy with.

A program can be:
- shorter.
- easier to read by a human.
- more correct around edge cases.
- faster than another which does the same thing.
- much easier to change when the requirements change.

These are sometimes in conflict.

Try writing a function in different ways and see which version is better.

Sometimes a program can log or assert to generate interesting observations which feed into further development of the program. We do our own science on the outputs later to improve the program.

When there are multiple good ways to implement something, especially involving state or the definition of a type: please ask the user. User loves AskUserQuestion, but please explain the problem correctly in the regular session before asking the question.

# Before committing

At the workspace root:

	cargo test

That includes the VM tests in tests/vm, which take minutes.  If the change can't affect anything they exercise (e.g. it's only to `reboop check`'s table), only compile them, and run just the unit tests:

	cargo test --no-run && cargo test --lib --bins

# Using git safely

**Other sessions may be staging and committing** here, including the files you are changing, and their edits can land between your last check and your commit. So, never use `git add FILE`, `git commit -a`, or `git commit -- FILES`. Instead, in the repository's top directory (elsewhere, a patch can silently miss files):

1. Write your changes to a patch, then remove any hunks that aren't yours:

		git diff --binary -- FILES > /tmp/NAME.patch

   `git diff` leaves out files that git doesn't track yet, so for each file you created, append:

		git diff --no-index --binary /dev/null NEW_FILE >> /tmp/NAME.patch

   This one exits with status 1 even on success, so don't chain it with `&&`.
2. If `git status` shows any change that you didn't make, run checks in a `git clone --shared` copy with only your patch applied.
3. Commit the patch through the index:

		git diff --cached --quiet && git apply --cached /tmp/NAME.patch && git commit -F /tmp/NAME.msg

   `git diff --cached --quiet` ensures no other session has staged anything, because `git commit` would commit that too. If `git apply` fails, HEAD has changed under your patch: remake it and test it again.

On HEAD, git rebase, amend, reset, stash, etc. **are never allowed**, unless other sessions are idle and not waiting on anything!

To change a commit message, use `git-reword COMMIT < NEW_FULL_MESSAGE`, not `git history reword` or an amend.

# Commit sizes and messages

Smaller changes are usually easier to think about. Commit one logical change at a time whenever possible! Commit early and often!

When small commits are too hard with e.g. the build still working, larger commits are fine.

**Use the imperative mood in the subject line**. Do not end the subject line with a period. Wrap the body at 72 characters, generally.

Sample subject line:

	Don't insert a file and rollback a transaction just to get the id
	Factor out file-reading function that looks up the storage
	Make sure zstd-compressed data round-trips back to input data
	Refactor some tests a bit
	Refactor to reduce repetition
	Resolve oxlint warning
	schema: forbid '.' and '..' in DOMAIN linux_basename; add more tests
	storage_read::read: don't require storage for size=0 files
	storage_write::write: don't hold a postgres transaction open while we upload a file
	storage_write::write: don't take a transaction as an argument
	Tweak comment
	Update Cargo.lock

Automatically commit your changes with this commit template:

	Subject line

	A longer description or explanation of why/what is changing, when it is genuinely helpful.

	Model-output: model name e.g. Claude Mythos 5.1

	Session-file: ~/.claude/projects/[...]/[...].jsonl

# Code review after each commit

After each commit made, get it reviewed by Codex and by Claude, all at xhigh reasoning, by running this in the repository, in one Bash call with `run_in_background` (the reviews can take many minutes):

	review-commits <sha>

If you made several commits, ensure reviews cover them all: either run `review-commits <sha>` once for each commit, or review the whole batch at once with `review-commits <sha before your first commit>..<sha of your last commit>`.

`review-commits` runs the reviewers in a `git clone --shared` of the repository, saves each review to ~/.ai-code-reviews/{model}/{full sha, or full range}, and prints every review. Once every reviewer has exited, it deletes the clone, and exits with status 1 if any reviewer failed.

Notes:

- Review findings are from **fallible machines eager to find issues**: think and prefer fixes that don't add a bunch of code we don't really need.
- Once all the reviews are in, fix the oversights that are really worth fixing, in logical, independent commits where possible, without "act on the ... reviews of ..."! If nothing, say briefly why the findings didn't warrant changes.
- Do _not_ send follow-up fixes through another review. (Exception: the follow-up grew into something substantial beyond addressing the findings.)
